cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-four-li.summary: Within a gold circle a youthful, haloed figure sits enthroned on a rainbow-like arc, holding a book and blessing, surrounded by the four winged living creatures — man, eagle, lion and calf — each holding a book; below, seven burning lamps stand above the sea of glass. In this cycle, as Wikipedia notes, Christ is shown as the beardless Logos enthroned.
facts: The Trier Apocalypse contains 74 full-page drawings illustrating about 150 episodes of the Book of Revelation; it is one of the earliest illustrated Apocalypse manuscripts to survive.
Its pictures are thought to copy a late antique model of the 4th–6th century, which explains features such as books shown as scrolls and Christ as the beardless Logos.
cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-four-li.notes: Folio not stated on the Commons file. The enthroned figure has a plain nimbus; its identification with Christ follows the manuscript's general practice.

cur:manuscripts-aethelwold-trinity-initi.summary: Inside a great gold initial O, a figure with a cross-nimbus sits enthroned on a rainbow, blessing with the right hand and holding a book, his green mantle falling in swirling folds. Beneath, gold capitals proclaim 'Trinitas unus et verus Deus, Pater et Filius et Spiritus Sanctus'. The one God of the Trinity is shown with the features and cross-halo of Christ.
facts: The Benedictional of St Æthelwold, written by the monk Godeman for Bishop Æthelwold of Winchester (963–984), is regarded as the masterpiece of late Anglo-Saxon illumination; it has 28 full-page miniatures.
The Latin inscription declares the Trinity to be one true God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit; the blessing is that for Trinity Sunday.
cur:manuscripts-aethelwold-trinity-initi.notes: The figure personifies the Triune God; it is given Christ's cross-nimbus, as was customary, but the image is a Trinity rather than a narrative depiction of Christ.

cur:manuscripts-escorial-john-before-the.summary: Beneath an arch, the haloed Lord sits enthroned with a book, surrounded by crowned elders and figures, while at the bottom John lies fallen beside the sea, where fish swim. A caption above refers to the vision 'like unto the Son of man'.
facts: The Escorial Beatus has 151 surviving leaves and 52 miniatures; it was probably made at San Millán de la Cogolla and was already in the Escorial library in the 16th century.
Its figures, with huge eyes and boldly patterned drapery, are among the most expressive in the Beatus tradition.
cur:manuscripts-escorial-john-before-the.notes: Folio not stated on the Commons file.
